commentary.bottom_line: Seventeen frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries endorse version and configuration control with re-review after material changes, but no study has tested whether this practice detects or prevents harmful changes. Three hazard studies show that template, coding, and prompt changes can shift performance.

perspectives.view: No study tests version control or change-triggered re-review. Three studies document the hazard: one quasi-experimental deployment study and two automated benchmarks. These show that the problem exists. They do not show that the safeguard works, so the evidence for the practice itself is absent and cannot be graded.

In one deployment with 66 providers, a note template configuration change reduced ICD-10 documentation accuracy from 79% to 35%. This suggests that changes outside the model itself can cause large drops in accuracy that go unnoticed. No study has examined whether change control would catch such a drop before it affects patients.

In a benchmark of 239,246 admissions, the ICD-9-to-ICD-10 coding transition acted as a dataset shift and was associated with performance degradation. A prompt-family change produced 3 reversals among 36 hardness pairs, with 91.7% agreement. These results suggest that data and prompt changes may belong in a change inventory. The staff burden of re-review has not been measured.

The prompt sensitivity benchmark included limited English proficiency or non-English trial populations and found 91.7% agreement across prompt families. No study examined Medicaid or safety-net settings. No study tested whether re-review after changes protects these groups. An obstetric equity commentary argues that configuration shifts can redistribute delays, but no study has tested this claim.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions asks manufacturers for installation and maintenance procedures. An EU AI Act tutorial calls for refreshing the technical file and rerunning conformance tests before redeployment. These sources set expectations for documenting changes. None of them reports outcomes from applying those expectations in health systems.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares health systems with and without version control and change-triggered re-review. Such a study would measure whether performance shifts are detected, how quickly they are found, and whether patients are harmed. Research should also measure the staff time that re-review requires and whether vendor-initiated updates are captured in local inventories.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tests the practice, so no test has included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard benchmark involved limited English proficiency or non-English populations, which suggests that prompt changes may affect these groups. Whether change control protects them is unknown.
